questions.prompt: Which two fields must every `Tool` object in a `tools/list` result carry, according to the specification's schema?

options.text: `name` and `description`
options.feedback: The description is the field a model leans on most, but the schema marks it optional; a tool without one is still a valid `Tool`.

options.text: `name` and `inputSchema`
options.feedback: These are the only two members without a `?` in the `Tool` interface: a tool needs an identifier to be called by and a schema for its arguments object.

options.text: `inputSchema` and `outputSchema`
options.feedback: `outputSchema` is optional. A tool may return only content blocks and publish no output schema at all, as `CallToolResult` returns do.

options.text: `name` and `title`
options.feedback: `title` is an optional display label for a user interface; when it is absent a host falls back to `annotations.title` and then to `name`.

questions.explanation: Section 2's table marks exactly two fields as required: `name`, the identifier a `tools/call` names, and `inputSchema`, a JSON Schema with `type: "object"` at the root. Everything else, including `description` and `outputSchema`, is optional.
hints: Look for the members of the `Tool` interface that carry no question mark.

questions.prompt: A tool is registered with `@mcp.tool()`, no flags, and annotated `-> Snapshot`, where `Snapshot` sets `self.cpu_percent` and `self.memory_percent` inside `__init__` and has no annotations in its class body. What does `mcp==2.3.0` do?

options.text: Registration fails with `InvalidSignature` at import, so the server process never starts serving.
options.feedback: That is what happens only when `structured_output=True` is passed. Without the flag the SDK accepts the class and says nothing.

options.text: It publishes a schema built from the type hints written on the `__init__` parameters instead.
options.feedback: Those are annotations on a function, not on the class. `get_type_hints()` on the class finds none, so no model is built.

options.text: It registers with `outputSchema: null`, and a call returns the object's `repr` as successful text.
options.feedback: The SDK's branch for an ordinary class leaves the model as `None`, so nothing is published, and the result is the serialized `repr`, a memory address marked as a success.

options.text: It logs a warning and publishes the result wrapped as `{"result": ...}`, as for a primitive.
options.feedback: Wrapping is for primitives and generics such as `str` or `list[str]`. For this class the SDK publishes nothing, and `snippets/silent_schema.py` counts zero SDK log records at INFO or above.

questions.explanation: Section 5 shows the SDK calling `get_type_hints()` on the return class; a class with no class-body annotations has none, the model stays `None`, and the tool registers without an output schema. The call then returns `"<__main__.Snapshot object at 0x...>"` as text, with no exception, warning, or log line.
hints: Ask where `get_type_hints()` looks for annotations when it is given a class.
Then ask which of the outcomes involves a flag the prompt says was not passed.

questions.prompt: Under `mcp==2.3.0`, a tool named `lookup` calls a helper that raises `KeyError('region')`, and nothing in the tool catches it. What does the model receive?

options.text: A JSON-RPC `error` object with code `-32603` (`Internal error`) and no result.
options.feedback: The high-level server turns every exception except `MCPError` into a result. Only `MCPError` travels as a JSON-RPC `error` object.

options.text: A result with `isError: true` whose text is `Error executing tool lookup: 'region'`.
options.feedback: That form, with the exception's text appended, is what a `ToolError` produces. An exception the tool did not anticipate is a crash, and its text stays on the server.

options.text: A result with `isError: true` whose only text is `Error executing tool lookup`.
options.feedback: Since 2.1.0 an exception other than `ToolError`, `ResourceError` or `MCPError` is a crash: the model gets the generic sentence, and the server logs the traceback at ERROR.

options.text: A result with `isError: false` and an empty `content` array.
options.feedback: A failure is never reported as a success. The SDK marks the result with `isError: true` so that a client can tell the model the call failed.

questions.explanation: Section 7's `average` tool divides by zero and the model receives `Error executing tool average` and nothing more, while the server logs `Tool 'average' raised an unexpected exception` with the traceback. Raising `ToolError` with a written sentence is how a tool gets its reason to the model.
hints: Ask whether `KeyError` is one of the exception types the SDK treats as a deliberate refusal.
Compare the text a `ToolError` produces with the text section 7 shows for the division by zero.

questions.prompt: A tool's entry in `tools/list` carries no `annotations` at all. Read with the defaults the specification gives each hint, how does that tool describe itself to a host?

options.text: Read-only, non-destructive, and confined to a closed world.
options.feedback: `readOnlyHint` defaults to `false` and `openWorldHint` to `true`. The defaults assume the worst, not the best.

options.text: Not read-only, possibly destructive, and interacting with an open world.
options.feedback: `readOnlyHint` defaults to `false`, `destructiveHint` and `openWorldHint` to `true`, so an undeclared tool is a destructive open-world tool.

options.text: Not read-only, but non-destructive and idempotent.
options.feedback: `destructiveHint` defaults to `true`, not `false`, and `idempotentHint` defaults to `false`.

options.text: Unclassified: a host must refuse to call any tool that arrives without annotations.
options.feedback: Annotations are optional and nothing requires a host to refuse. The defaults exist precisely so that a missing hint still has a meaning.

questions.explanation: Section 8's table gives the defaults: `readOnlyHint` false, `destructiveHint` true, `idempotentHint` false, `openWorldHint` true. Two of them default to the cautious answer, so a tool that declares nothing reads as destructive and open-world, and only its author can claim otherwise. Even then the claim is a hint the host must treat as untrusted unless the server is trusted.
hints: Ask what a host should assume about a tool whose author has made no claim at all.
The specification's defaults are chosen so that silence never sounds safe.

questions.prompt: `get_system_info` takes no parameters. Which statement about its `inputSchema` is correct for revision 2026-07-28 and `mcp==2.3.0`?

options.text: A tool with no parameters may omit `inputSchema`, and the SDK leaves it out.
options.feedback: `inputSchema` is required on every tool, parameters or not, and the SDK always publishes one.

options.text: The SDK publishes `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false}`, the form the Tools page recommends.
options.feedback: That is the form the Tools page recommends, but it is not what the SDK emits; none of the decorator's parameters produces it.

options.text: `inputSchema` may be `null` for such a tool, since there is no argument to validate at all.
options.feedback: The schema must be a valid JSON Schema object with `type: "object"` at the root; `null` is not allowed.

options.text: The SDK publishes an object schema with empty `properties`: legal, but not the recommended form.
options.feedback: `snippets/input_schema.py` prints `{"type": "object", "properties": {}, "title": "get_system_infoArguments"}`: permissive, legal, and short of the `additionalProperties: false` form the Tools page recommends.

questions.explanation: Section 3 quotes the Tools page's two valid forms for a parameterless tool, with `additionalProperties: false` recommended and the plain object schema permitted, and prints what the SDK publishes for `get_system_info`, which is the permissive kind.
hints: `inputSchema` is one of the two required fields, so first rule out the options that drop it.
Then compare the recommended form with what the snippet prints.

questions.prompt: A tool is registered with `@mcp.tool()` on a function annotated `-> list[str]` that returns `["a", "b"]`. In one sentence: what shape does the published `outputSchema` describe, and what `structuredContent` does a call carry?

answer.model: An object with one required property, `result`, holding the array of strings, so the call carries `{"result": ["a", "b"]}` rather than a top-level array.

questions.explanation: Section 4's table, measured by `snippets/output_schema.py`, wraps `list[...]` returns: the schema is an object with a required `result` property, and the call carries `{"result": ["a", "b"]}`. A top-level array is legal in the protocol but needs a hand-built `CallToolResult`.
hints: Lists, unions and primitives share one treatment in the SDK's table.

questions.prompt: A tool must refuse a `region` argument that names a region the server does not serve, and the model should read the reason and retry. Under `mcp==2.3.0`, which exception should the tool raise, and what does the model receive if the tool raises a plain `ValueError` instead?

answer.model: Raise `ToolError` (from `mcp.server.mcpserver.exceptions`). A plain `ValueError` is treated as a crash, so the model gets only `Error executing tool <name>` in an `isError` result, without the reason.
accept: ^(?![\s\S]*`?toolerror`?\s+(?:is|are|counts\s+as|becomes|would\s+be|is\s+treated\s+as|gets\s+treated\s+as)\s+(?:a\s+|an\s+)?(?:crash|unexpected|generic))(?![\s\S]*\b(?:should|must|to)\s+raise\s+(?:a\s+|an\s+)?(?:plain\s+)?`?valueerror)(?!\W*`?valueerror\b)(?![\s\S]*\b(?:maybe|perhaps|probably|possibly|might|not sure|unsure|i think|i guess)\b)(?![\s\S]*\b(?:not|never|n't|instead of|rather than)\s+(?:a\s+|an\s+|the\s+|use\s+|raise\s+|raising\s+|using\s+)?`?toolerror)(?![\s\S]*\braise\s+(?:an?\s+)?`?mcperror)(?=[\s\S]*\btoolerror\b)(?=[\s\S]*(?:\bcrash|\bgeneric\b|\bonly\b[^.]{0,40}error executing tool|without (?:the|its|any) (?:message|text|reason|detail)|\b(?:message|text|reason|detail)s?\b[^.]{0,30}\b(?:hidden|lost|dropped|swallowed|stays?|kept|withheld|not (?:sent|shown|passed|included))|never (?:sees|reads|gets) the (?:message|text|reason)|unexpected exception))[\s\S]{25,}$

questions.explanation: Section 7 shows both: `ToolError` reaches the model as `Error executing tool sample_window: <the sentence>`, while an exception the tool did not anticipate is a crash, and the model reads only `Error executing tool average` while the traceback stays in the server's log.
hints: One exception class is the SDK's signal for an anticipated failure whose message the model should read.
Compare what section 7 printed for `sample_window` with what it printed for `average`.

questions.prompt: The redesigned `find_process` publishes `limit` with `minimum` 1 and `maximum` 50. A model calls it with `{"name": "python", "limit": 500}`. In one or two sentences: what comes back, and does the function body run?

answer.model: A result with `isError: true` whose text is a validation error saying `limit` should be less than or equal to 50; the arguments are rejected before the call, so the body never runs.
accept: ^(?![\s\S]*\b(?:maybe|perhaps|probably|possibly|might|not sure|unsure|i think|i guess)\b)(?![\s\S]*(?<!not\s)(?<!not\sa\s)(?<!no\s)(?<!than\sa\s)\b(?:protocol(?:-level)?\serror|json-rpc\serror|error\sobject))(?![\s\S]*(?<!not\s)(?<!no\s)-32602)(?![\s\S]*(?<!not\s)(?<!no\s)(?<!n't\s)(?<!never\s)\bclamp)(?![\s\S]*(?<!before\sthe\s)(?<!before\s)(?<!until\sthe\s)\b(?:body|function|it)\s+(?:does\s+|still\s+)?runs?\b(?!\s+(?:at all|first)))(?=[\s\S]*(?:is_?error|error result|execution error|validation error|tool error|an?\s+error))(?=[\s\S]*(?:\b50\b|less than or equal|maximum|\bbound|out of range|too (?:large|big|high)))(?=[\s\S]*(?:\b(?:never|not|n't)\b[^.;]{0,25}\b(?:run|runs|reached|reach|reaches|execut\w*|called|invoked)|\bbefore\b[^.;]{0,30}\b(?:body|function|call|runs?)|\bno\b[^.;]{0,10}\b(?:body|function)))[\s\S]{20,}$

questions.explanation: Section 3's script calls the redesigned tool with `limit` 500 and prints `isError: true` with `Input should be less than or equal to 50`: the SDK validates arguments against the published schema's model before the function runs. The project's original `find_process`, which has no bound in its schema, clamps inside the body instead.
hints: Ask what the SDK does with the arguments before it calls the function.
Arguments that fail validation are an execution error in this SDK, not a JSON-RPC error.

questions.prompt: A tool is registered with `@mcp.tool()` on `def book(city: str, nights: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=30)], guests: int = 2, plan: Literal["room", "half", "full"] = "room") -> str`. Across all properties of the published `inputSchema`, how many `minimum`, `maximum` and `enum` keywords appear in total?
questions.precision_note: Closed form: ge and le each become one keyword on nights (minimum 1, maximum 30) and the Literal becomes one enum on plan; city and guests carry none. Confirmed against mcp==2.3.0, which publishes nights with maximum 30 and minimum 1 and plan with enum ["room", "half", "full"].
questions.explanation: `Field(ge=1, le=30)` becomes `minimum` 1 and `maximum` 30 on `nights`, and the `Literal` becomes an `enum` on `plan`, as the redesigned `find_process` in section 3 showed for `limit` and `sort_by`. `guests` has only a default and `city` only a type, so the total is 3.
hints: Each Pydantic bound maps to one JSON Schema keyword.
Count `ge` and `le` separately, and remember that a default is not a bound.

questions.prompt: Eight tools are registered with `@mcp.tool()` and no flags under `mcp==2.3.0`, annotated `-> str`, `-> list[int]`, `-> TextContent`, `-> Image`, `-> CallToolResult`, `-> Plain` (a class that sets `self.x` only in `__init__`), `-> Point` (a dataclass with `x: int` and `y: int`), and one with no return annotation. How many of the eight publish a non-null `outputSchema`?
questions.precision_note: Section 4's table (snippets/output_schema.py): str and list[int] are wrapped, the dataclass has its own schema, the other five publish none. Confirmed by registering exactly these eight under mcp==2.3.0.
questions.explanation: `-> str` and `-> list[int]` are wrapped, and the dataclass `Point` becomes its own schema: three. A content block and the `Image` helper publish nothing since release 2.1.0, a bare `CallToolResult` leaves the result to the tool, `Plain` has no class-body annotations, and no annotation means no schema.
hints: Sort the eight into wrapped, own schema, and none, using the table in section 4.
Content blocks changed in release 2.1.0, and a class needs annotations in its body.

questions.prompt: Write `respond(request_id, outcome)`, which returns, as a dict, the JSON-RPC response a revision 2026-07-28 server sends to one request (leave out `_meta`). `outcome` is one of: `("unknown_method", method)`, answered with code `-32601`, message `"Method not found"` and `data` set to the method; `("arguments_not_object",)`, answered with code `-32602`; `("tool_failed", text)`, for a tool that ran and failed with that text; and `("ok", data)`, for a tool that returned `data` as structured content, with the serialized JSON in one text block as the Tools page asks. Every result carries `resultType` `"complete"` and an explicit `isError`. Use only the standard library.
questions.starter:
import json


def respond(request_id, outcome):
    """Return the JSON-RPC response (without _meta) a server sends to one request."""
    raise NotImplementedError
questions.tests:
import json

r = respond(5, ("unknown_method", "tools/nonexistent"))
assert r["jsonrpc"] == "2.0" and r["id"] == 5
assert "result" not in r, "a protocol error carries no result"
assert r["error"]["code"] == -32601, r
assert r["error"].get("data") == "tools/nonexistent"
assert r["error"]["message"] == "Method not found", r

r = respond(7, ("arguments_not_object",))
assert r["jsonrpc"] == "2.0" and r["id"] == 7 and "result" not in r
assert r["error"]["code"] == -32602, r

r = respond(4, ("tool_failed", "seconds must be between 1 and 30, got 500. Retry with a value in range."))
assert "error" not in r, "a tool that ran and failed is not a protocol error"
assert r["jsonrpc"] == "2.0" and r["id"] == 4
res = r["result"]
assert res["isError"] is True
assert res["content"] == [{"type": "text", "text": "seconds must be between 1 and 30, got 500. Retry with a value in range."}]
assert res["resultType"] == "complete"

r = respond(3, ("ok", {"rows": 12000}))
assert "error" not in r and r["jsonrpc"] == "2.0" and r["id"] == 3
res = r["result"]
assert res["isError"] is False
assert res["structuredContent"] == {"rows": 12000}
assert len(res["content"]) == 1 and res["content"][0]["type"] == "text"
assert json.loads(res["content"][0]["text"]) == {"rows": 12000}, "the text block carries the serialized structured content"
assert res["resultType"] == "complete"
print("all respond tests passed")
questions.explanation: An unknown method and an `arguments` value that breaks the shape of `CallToolRequest` are protocol errors, so they get an `error` member and no `result`, as the first server answered in section 7. A tool that ran and failed gets a successful result with `isError: true` and its message in a text block, so a client can hand it to the model. A success carries `structuredContent` and, for clients that do not read it, the same JSON serialized in a text block, which is what the SDK did for `find_process` in section 4.
hints: Decide first which outcomes get an `error` member and which get a `result`.
Only a result carries `isError`; for success, put `json.dumps(data)` in the text block beside `structuredContent`.

questions.prompt: Write `missing_output_schemas(listing)`, which takes a parsed `tools/list` result (a dict with a `tools` list in the wire spelling) and returns the sorted names of the tools that publish no output schema: those whose `outputSchema` is absent or JSON `null`. An empty object `{}` is a valid JSON Schema that accepts any value, so a tool publishing it counts as having a schema. Use only the standard library.
questions.tests:
import json

wire = """{"resultType": "complete", "ttlMs": 0, "cacheScope": "private", "tools": [
  {"name": "get_system_info", "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}},
   "outputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"cpu_percent": {"type": "number"}}}},
  {"name": "silent", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}, "outputSchema": null},
  {"name": "raw_array", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}},
  {"name": "anything", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}, "outputSchema": {}},
  {"name": "loud", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}, "outputSchema": {"type": "object"}}
]}"""
listing = json.loads(wire)
got = missing_output_schemas(listing)
assert got == ["raw_array", "silent"], got
assert missing_output_schemas({"tools": []}) == []
assert missing_output_schemas({"tools": [{"name": "z", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}},
                                         {"name": "a", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}}]}) == ["a", "z"]
print("all missing_output_schemas tests passed")
questions.explanation: This is the project's `test_every_tool_publishes_an_output_schema` rewritten over the wire form: a missing key and an explicit `null` both mean nothing was published, while `{}` is a real, permissive schema. Looking the key up with a default handles the absent case, and comparing with `None` rather than testing truthiness keeps `{}` on the published side.
hints: `dict.get` with no default returns `None` for an absent key, the same value JSON `null` parses to.
An empty dict is falsy in Python, so a truthiness test would treat `{}` as missing.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom a server author sees under `mcp==2.3.0` with its cause.

left.text: The model receives `Error executing tool average` and nothing else.
The client raises `RuntimeError: Invalid structured content returned by tool celsius: 'units' is a required property`.
A tool lists with `outputSchema: null` and returns `"<__main__.Snapshot object at 0x...>"` as text.
The server's standard error shows `Tool name contains invalid characters: '/'` at startup.
A misspelled tool name comes back as `isError: true` with `Unknown tool: find_procss`.

right.text: The return class has no annotations in its class body.
An exception other than `ToolError` escaped the tool body.
The SDK's tool manager raises `ToolError` for a name it does not have.
The structured content does not fit the schema the client holds for that tool.
A tool name uses a character outside the set the specification advises.
The tool body raised `MCPError` with code `-32602`.

questions.explanation: A bare exception is a crash whose text stays on the server. The client's `RuntimeError` is its own check of `structuredContent` against the published schema. A null schema with a `repr` is the class without class-body annotations. The slash warning comes from `mcp.shared.tool_name_validation` at registration. The unknown name is the SDK's divergence from the Tools page's `-32602`. An `MCPError` would reach the client as a JSON-RPC `error` object, which none of the symptoms is.
hints: Separate what the model reads, what the client raises, and what the server logs.
An `MCPError` produces an `error` member; check which of the symptoms, if any, is a protocol error.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of one successful `tools/call` through an `mcp==2.3.0` server and the SDK's client in the order they happen, for a tool annotated with a dataclass return type.

items.text: The server checks the arguments against the tool's input model.
The client checks `structuredContent` against the `outputSchema` it cached from `tools/list`.
The server looks the tool up by the `name` in the request.
The server turns the return value into a text block and `structuredContent`, checked against the output model.

questions.explanation: A name the server does not have fails before anything else (`Unknown tool: ...`). Arguments are validated before the body runs, which is why a `limit` of 500 never reached the redesigned `find_process`. The return value is converted and checked on the server, which is where a hand-built result that misses a required field becomes `Error executing tool reading`, and the client's own check of the published schema comes last, on its side of the wire.
hints: An unknown name and invalid arguments are both reported without the body running; which must be known first?
The client can only check what has already crossed the wire.

questions.prompt: A colleague's booking tool raises `MCPError(INVALID_PARAMS, "bad date")` when the requested check-in date is in the past, arguing that a past date is an invalid parameter and that `-32602` (`Invalid params`) is therefore the honest code. Critique the choice against the Tools page and the SDK's behavior, and rewrite the failure so the model can recover.
questions.solution:
The choice puts a tool execution error on the protocol side. The Tools page draws the line by what failed: an unknown tool, a request that breaks the shape of `CallToolRequest`, and server errors are protocol errors, while API failures, input validation errors such as a date in the wrong range, and business-logic refusals are execution errors returned as a successful result with `isError: true`. A past date is a well-formed request that is wrong for the tool, so it belongs on the execution side, which is also where SEP-1303 moved input validation errors so that a model can fix them.

The practical cost is the important part. `MCPError` is the one exception the SDK's tool layer re-raises untouched, so the client receives a JSON-RPC `error` object. The Tools page says clients **should** hand execution errors to the model and only **may** hand it protocol errors, which are less likely to lead to recovery; a host may never show the model the text at all. And `bad date` names neither the constraint nor the value nor the fix.

The rewrite raises `ToolError` with a sentence the model can act on, for example `ToolError(f"check_in must be today or later, got {check_in}. Today is {today}. Retry with a future date.")`. The SDK turns that into `isError: true` with `Error executing tool book: check_in must be today or later, ...`, logs it at INFO, and a model can retry with a corrected argument. If the bound can be expressed in the schema (a format, a minimum) it should also go there, so the first attempt is more likely to be right.

rubric.criterion: Places a past date on the execution-error side using the Tools page's split between request-shape failures and failures of the work.
Explains that MCPError becomes a JSON-RPC error object that clients need not show the model, so recovery is unlikely.
Rewrites the failure as ToolError with the constraint, the offending value and the correction, and states it arrives as isError true.
Notes that the message bad date gives the model nothing to change, or suggests moving an expressible bound into the schema.

questions.explanation: Section 7 sets out the split and the SDK's three paths: `ToolError` for an anticipated failure, a crash for any other exception, and `MCPError` for a real protocol error, which a well-written tool body rarely decides.
hints: Ask whether the request itself was malformed or whether the work could not be done with a well-formed request.
Then ask which of the two channels the Tools page says clients should pass to the model.

questions.prompt: A host connects two servers, configured under the keys `files` and `web`. Both expose a tool named `search`; `web` also exposes `fetch`, which no other server has; and both servers report the name `search-server` in their `serverInfo`. Design the tool names the host shows the model, and justify each choice against the Tools page's naming rules and its guidance on collisions.
questions.solution:
Only the contested name is qualified, and on both sides: `files.search` and `web.search`, while `fetch` keeps its bare name. The Tools page scopes uniqueness to one server and says a client that aggregates tools **should** have a disambiguation strategy such as a server prefix; qualifying only what collides keeps every uncontested name in the form a model may already know.

The prefix comes from the host's own configuration keys, `files` and `web`, because the page says a server's self-reported name is not guaranteed unique and **should not** be relied upon for disambiguation. Here both servers report `search-server`, so a prefix built from `serverInfo` would produce two identical names and solve nothing.

The separator is a dot because the qualified name has to stay inside the character set the page advises: ASCII letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot, 1 to 128 characters. A slash is outside it, and the Python SDK logs a validation warning for `files/search`. Where a model provider forbids the dot, the host falls back to an underscore, `files_search`, never to a slash. Post 11 builds exactly this catalog.

rubric.criterion: Qualifies only the colliding search names, on both servers, and leaves fetch bare, with a reason.
Takes the prefix from the host's configuration keys and rejects serverInfo names because they are not guaranteed unique and here collide.
Uses a dot separator, or an underscore where a provider forbids the dot, and rules out the slash with the advised character set.
States that uniqueness is scoped to one server, so the host, not the servers, owns the collision.

questions.explanation: Section 9 states the naming rules and the collision guidance, and post 11 turns them into a host's catalog; the two together decide the prefix source, the separator and which names to qualify.
hints: Start from who can guarantee a unique prefix: the servers, or the host's own configuration.
Then check each candidate separator against the advised character set.

questions.prompt: A tool is annotated `-> Annotated[CallToolResult, Reading]`, where `Reading` is a dataclass with required fields `value` and `units`, and its body returns a hand-built result whose `structured_content` is `{"value": 21.5}`. What does an SDK client receive under `mcp==2.3.0`?

options.text: A result with `isError: true` saying only `Error executing tool reading`; the server logs an ERROR.
options.feedback: The server checks a hand-built result against the annotated model before sending it, and the failure is treated as a crash, so the generic sentence is all that crosses the wire.

options.text: A conforming-looking result, after which the client raises `RuntimeError` naming the missing `units` field.
options.feedback: The client's check never sees this result: the server's own check fails first and replaces it with an `isError` result, which the client does not validate.

options.text: The result exactly as built, because a `CallToolResult` return bypasses every schema check.
options.feedback: Only a bare `-> CallToolResult` skips the output model. `Annotated[CallToolResult, Reading]` publishes the schema of `Reading` and holds the result to it.

options.text: A JSON-RPC `error` object with code `-32603` (`Internal error`).
options.feedback: The SDK reports a failed output check as a tool result with `isError: true`, not as a protocol error.

questions.explanation: Section 12 shows both checks. `snippets/output_schema.py` prints `isError: true, text: 'Error executing tool reading'` and `server log: ERROR Tool 'reading' raised an unexpected exception` for exactly this tool; the client's `RuntimeError` appears only when the published schema itself stops fitting data the server considers valid.
hints: Ask which side holds the `Reading` model at the moment the result is built.

questions.prompt: A tool `get_logs(service: str, level: str, n: int = 100) -> str` has the docstring "Get logs. level is one of debug, info, warning, error; n is at most 500." Models often call it with `level` set to `"WARN"` or `n` set to 10,000. Redesign the signature and the docstring with the SDK so that the published `inputSchema` and description carry what the model needs, describe the properties it then publishes, and say what a model that still sends `n` 10,000 gets back.
questions.solution:
Move each constraint out of the docstring and into the parameter it constrains, with `Annotated` and Pydantic's `Field`:

```python
@mcp.tool()
def get_logs(
    service: Annotated[str, Field(description="Service name as it appears in the deployment, for example 'checkout'.")],
    level: Annotated[Literal["debug", "info", "warning", "error"], Field(description="Lowest severity to include.")] = "warning",
    n: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=500, description="Most recent lines to return.")] = 100,
) -> str:
    """Return the most recent log lines of one service, newest last. Use it to see why a service is failing; it does not search across services."""
```

The published schema then gives `level` an `enum` of the four strings, so `"WARN"` is no longer something the model can invent without breaking a visible rule; gives `n` a `minimum` of 1, a `maximum` of 500 and its default; and gives every property a `description`, which the SDK never builds from an `Args:` block. The tool description says what the tool is for and what it does not do.

A model that still sends `n` 10,000 gets a result with `isError: true` whose text is the validation error, `Input should be less than or equal to 500`, and the function body never runs. That message names the bound, so the next attempt can succeed. Choosing a default for `level` is a design decision; leaving it required is also defensible if the caller must always choose.

rubric.criterion: Uses a Literal (or equivalent enum) for level and Field bounds ge=1, le=500 for n.
Gives each property a description in Field, not only in the docstring.
Describes the published properties: enum, minimum, maximum, default, description.
States that n of 10,000 returns an isError validation result naming the bound, before the body runs.
Rewrites the tool description to say what the tool does and when to use it, or what it does not do.
